content.title: Europe After Russia's Invasion of Ukraine – A New Security Reality
content.description: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has reshaped Europe’s security landscape, prompting countries to strengthen defence, deepen cooperation, and reassess preparedness. How will this redefine Europe’s future security order, stability, and partnerships—and what role can trade play in this?
content.extendedDescription:
Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has significantly reshaped Europe’s security landscape. The war has affected relations between countries, intensified the focus on defense and preparedness, and led to new forms of international cooperation. At the same time, the question of Europe’s long-term security order has become increasingly important.

This panel will examine how the war in Ukraine is influencing European security policy and the implications for the future. The discussion will address issues such as military and political cooperation, trade, support for Ukraine, and how European countries are adapting their security strategies in an era of growing uncertainty.
speakerTitles: Partner Defence and Security, former UK Ambassador to Sweden

content.title: Logistics and aid transport in wartime – support for Ukraine in practice
content.description: Delivering humanitarian aid in a country at war requires complex logistics and coordination. Transport, security and access to the right resources affect whether aid gets through. How are aid deliveries to Ukraine organised, and what challenges arise in wartime?
content.extendedDescription:
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, humanitarian support from international actors, organisations and volunteer initiatives has been vital in helping civilians. Getting medicines, equipment, vehicles and other essential resources to a country at war requires advanced logistics, functioning transport routes and close cooperation between different actors.

The panel focuses on how aid deliveries to Ukraine are organised in practice and the challenges that arise when aid must be delivered in a conflict zone. The discussion highlights planning, security and coordination, and how organisations work to ensure that aid reaches those who need it most.

The discussion also explores the experience gained during the war and how it can contribute to better humanitarian logistics and cooperation in future crises.

content.title: How do we get construction and essential energy renovations moving?
content.description: The construction sector faces a critical challenge. Although it accounts for around 11% of Sweden’s GDP and is therefore central to both growth and societal development, neither construction nor essential energy renovations have got under way at the pace required. The EU’s new directives set clear requirements.
content.extendedDescription:
The EU’s energy efficiency requirements (EED & EPBD) are not just about climate ambitions, but now also about stronger preparedness and a more resilient society.
Much is currently at a standstill, while pressure to modernise, transform and renovate is growing rapidly.

The event explores why construction and energy renovations have not yet gathered pace, and the barriers, opportunities and solutions in a situation marked by uncertainty. We discuss the new requirements, why they exist and how they contribute both to the climate transition and to the resilience of Sweden’s building stock.

Discussions between business representatives and leading members of parliament bring different perspectives on how construction and renovation processes can be stimulated. The focus is on how the industry, politicians and other actors can jointly create the conditions to get the construction and energy renovations needed for Sweden’s future under way.

content.title: If the power goes out: how do households and society manage heating and cooking?
content.description: A prolonged power outage quickly removes the ability to heat homes and cook food. At the same time, many households lack alternative solutions. How can society reduce vulnerability and strengthen preparedness so that people can manage heating and cooking even when the electricity fails?
content.extendedDescription:
The security situation in Europe, growing cyber threats and a more vulnerable energy system have made civil preparedness increasingly relevant. Authorities urge households to be self-sufficient for at least a week in a crisis – but how many can actually heat their home or cook food if the power goes out?

In a society where almost every everyday function depends on electricity, a prolonged power outage risks quickly creating major problems. Without electricity, cookers, heating systems and many of the solutions we take for granted in everyday life stop working. At the same time, many households lack simple, practical alternatives for heating and cooking.

How well prepared are Swedish households really? What responsibility lies with individuals and what with society? And what solutions are needed to strengthen household preparedness in a more uncertain world?

Please visit our stand, where we present preparedness solutions and offer opportunities to ask questions and get more detailed information.
content.subject: Security/defence

content.title: Journalism from the frontline – reporting on war
content.description: Reporting on the war in Ukraine involves major risks. Journalists work close to the frontline under fire, facing threats and uncertain conditions to document the war. How does this affect journalism, and why is reporting from the scene crucial to the outside world’s understanding?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has made journalism one of the most dangerous professions in conflict zones. Journalists reporting from the frontline often work in dangerous and unpredictable conditions, facing the risk of shelling, attacks and other security threats. Despite this, their work plays a crucial role in documenting the war and giving the outside world a picture of what is happening on the ground.

The panel focuses on the challenges journalists face when reporting from an active war. The discussion highlights security, working conditions and how journalists navigate between the need for rapid reporting and the requirement for accurate, responsible journalism.

The discussion also explores how reporting from the scene affects the outside world’s understanding of the war, and why independent journalism is especially important in times of conflict and information influence operations.
content.subject: Media/journalism

content.title: Rehabilitation after war injuries – how can Sweden support Ukraine?
content.description: The war in Ukraine has created a major need for long-term rehabilitation for civilians and soldiers with severe injuries. International support is crucial. How can Swedish healthcare and rehabilitation expertise contribute to recovery and a better quality of life for those injured in war?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has created a major need for long-term rehabilitation for people injured in the war. Many civilians and soldiers live with serious physical injuries, amputations and trauma that require advanced medical treatment and long-term rehabilitation. Regaining function, independence and quality of life requires both medical expertise and effective rehabilitation systems.

The panel focuses on how international cooperation can strengthen rehabilitation for people injured in the war in Ukraine, and the role Swedish healthcare and rehabilitation expertise can play. The discussion highlights the need for long-term support, knowledge exchange and the development of rehabilitation services for people affected by the war.

The discussion also explores which experiences can contribute to developing rehabilitation care in crisis and conflict situations.

content.title: The changing role of women in Ukraine’s wartime economy
content.description: Russia’s full-scale invasion reshaped women’s roles in Ukraine. Women became combatants, led businesses, and entered transport, construction, logistics, and manufacturing. How does reconstruction create an opportunity to strengthen and sustain this workforce inclusion?
content.extendedDescription:
Since the start of the full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s labour market and social roles have changed rapidly. Severe staff shortages pushed women into male-dominated sectors, including transport, construction, logistics, infrastructure, manufacturing and technical jobs vital for wartime resilience and reconstruction.
These changes reflect a wider transformation. More than 68,000 women now serve in the Ukrainian military, including around 5000 in combat zones, while nearly one-third of Ukrainian companies are led by women. For many entering these fields was driven by economic pressure, displacement, and wartime realities. At the same time, these experiences are reshaping perceptions of competence and women’s roles in society.
The panel will explore how war is changing workforce participation and gender roles in Ukraine, what this means for reconstruction and the labour market and how international organisations, industry, and civil society can support long-term inclusion in these sectors.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: Human or machine – what shapes our inner compass?
content.description: With AI now a reality, human encounters are even more important. Have we lost the art of constructive conversation? Even in a polarised debate, reason, attentiveness and respect are needed to keep the focus on the issue rather than personal attacks.
content.extendedDescription: AI is here to stay. It will affect working life, how we acquire knowledge and how we see the world. What is true, what is reasonable and what is desirable are questions we must ask. What is human consciousness, as opposed to AI? Interaction with others is essential if our humanity is not to be forgotten. We therefore need a culture of conversation characterised by respect and civility, where different voices can be heard.

content.title: Unacceptable municipal implementation of LSS
content.description: What happens when municipalities breach LSS, even though it is a law establishing individual rights? Is support withheld? Are rights and court rulings ignored? And what does this mean for individuals’ self-determination and freedom?
content.extendedDescription:
The Parliamentary Ombudsman submitted the annual report for 2024 to the Riksdag’s Committee on the Constitution on 13 March 2025 with a clear message: shortcomings in municipalities’ implementation of LSS are completely unacceptable.

The Parliamentary Ombudsman receives around 200 complaints about municipal LSS services each year. The criticism is recurring: municipalities delay processing for months and years, disregard court rulings, reduce support without any change in needs, and treat a law establishing rights more like a recommendation.

For individuals, this is not merely a legal issue; it can be a question of living freely or in an institution. Every month without the right support is a month without participation, self-determination and the opportunity to live like others. When municipalities fail to act in accordance with LSS as a law establishing rights, many people entitled to support risk receiving none, or less than they are entitled to.
speakerTitles: Head of the Social Services Section

content.title: Is societal preparedness for peace not as important as preparedness for war?
content.description: Today we talk a great deal about preparedness for war, and the threats need to be taken seriously. But how prepared is our society to preserve peace? What economic benefits could we create by investing more in empathy, dialogue, education, trust and the courage to speak out against provocation and violence?
content.extendedDescription:
We need strong defence to deter war and defend society if war comes. At the same time, we still live in peace, and peace does not sustain itself.

War brings enormous costs in human suffering, resources and money. That is why we also need to discuss the part of societal preparedness concerned with preventing conflicts, strengthening social cohesion and building resilience against polarisation and violence.

What happens if we invest more in preserving peace? How can we strengthen society’s capacity for peace, and which actors need to contribute? Welcome to a discussion about peace as an active part of our societal preparedness.

content.title: Why wear a cloak of possibility? Consciously choosing to make a positive difference
content.description: Research on enclothed cognition shows that clothing and symbols can influence how we think, feel and act. What happens when we consciously choose to wear a cloak of possibility that reminds us of our responsibility, our agency and our ability to contribute to positive societal development?
content.extendedDescription:
Perhaps you have seen us in Almedalen wearing our cloaks and wondered why we wear them?

In this interactive session, we explore how identity, narratives and symbols influence human action. Inspired by Stellan Nordahl’s work Medvetna val: Från offerkofta till möjlighetsmantel and research on enclothed cognition, we examine how what we wear on our bodies can influence how we think, feel and act.

Can a cloak of possibility serve as a daily reminder to choose opportunities over despair, responsibility over resignation and action over passivity? Can personal symbols help us become more aware of the choices we make and the difference we want to make in the world?

Welcome to discover why we wear our cloaks, and what can happen when people choose to wear their possibilities rather than their limitations.

content.title: Energy communities – a new path towards the sustainable energy system of the future
content.description: The EU wants the number of electricity communities to increase by 2030, and Sweden is expected to change its rules. What opportunities do we want the legislation to provide?
content.extendedDescription: Today we see three forms of electricity community. One operates within a property through direct physical sharing. Another is an energy cooperative where members invest in a shared solar or wind installation and sell the surplus on the market. The third consists of concession-exempt grids (IKN) or microgrids, where several buildings or properties are connected using solar panels, batteries, smart controls and software that manages the installation. This allows electricity to be sold or shared between participating buildings and enables them to operate jointly across multiple markets through their regular grid connections. There is currently a requirement for each property to have a connection to the concession-regulated grid before its building or buildings may be connected to an IKN grid. Will the legislation also allow capacity in concession-regulated grids to be rented for IKN?
speakerTitles: Chair of Energikontoren Sverige, Professor of Industrial Energy Policy

content.title: How can we increase cooperation and dialogue between municipalities and private providers?
content.description: Procurement and privately delivered health and social care under the Social Services Act (SoL) and the Act concerning Support and Service for Persons with Certain Functional Impairments (LSS) – how do we increase cooperation so that we can complement one another and set appropriate requirements?
content.extendedDescription:
According to Upphandlingsmyndigheten, more than 17 000 public procurement notices are published each year. Health and social care accounts for the largest share of the total estimated value of public purchasing, around 34 per cent. The total value of public purchasing in Sweden exceeds SEK 1 000 billion annually.

There is a general perception that procurement focuses too heavily on the lowest price, sets unclear quality requirements and lacks adequate contract follow-up. How can we make procurement more quality-focused, designed around providers’ circumstances and based on relevant requirements? Is this possible, and what might it look like?

content.title: What does a functioning democracy require?
content.description: Democracy faces complex challenges in a time of rapid change, technological development, growing polarisation and declining trust.
content.extendedDescription:
“A generative dialogue about democracy.”
The future of democracy is not a finished story – it is shaped every day by how we talk, listen, learn and act together. In this unique session, participants come together in a special format: a generative dialogue we have named Glass Bead Games – a training session in collective wisdom. Here, we explore democracy’s path forward through active listening, conscious choices, generative dialogue and the joint creation of perspectives.

The format uses small groups in which each participant speaks for one minute at a time without interruption, followed by reflection and shared sensemaking.

content.description: As trust in institutions, the media and one another declines, making collective decisions becomes harder. What is needed to build shared understanding around direction, responsibility and common goals in a time marked by polarisation and information overload?
content.extendedDescription:
Humanity’s greatest challenges are not only technical or economic – they also concern our ability to build shared understanding. Without common frames of reference, trust and a sense of shared purpose, societies risk fragmenting and becoming trapped in conflict, paralysis and short-term thinking.
This panel examines how shared understanding emerges between people, organisations and societal systems. Which narratives, values and experiences make cooperation possible? How do digitalisation, AI and information warfare affect our collective perception of reality?
We also explore whether future societies need new forms of knowledge creation and meaning-making in which more perspectives can coexist without losing the ability to cooperate. Could building shared understanding become a key skill for democracy, peace and long-term sustainability? And how do we create a common direction without losing diversity and critical thinking?

content.title: Energy systems under attack – what can Sweden learn from Ukraine?
content.description: The war in Ukraine has shown how vulnerable energy systems can be when infrastructure becomes a target for attacks. At the same time, the country has developed ways to maintain energy supplies under extreme pressure. What lessons can other countries learn to strengthen energy security and resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has shown how vulnerable energy systems become when power plants, electricity grids and critical infrastructure come under attack. But it has also demonstrated how crucial robust energy systems, rapid restoration, decentralised solutions, backup power and local electricity preparedness are when society’s functions are placed under extreme pressure. From transmission grids and technical infrastructure to smaller safety and charging points close to people, energy security is also about the ability to communicate, receive healthcare, reach shelters and help both oneself and others.
What can Sweden learn from Ukraine to strengthen energy security, civil preparedness and resilience, from national infrastructure to individuals’ ability to act?

content.title: The Temporary Protection Directive in practice – reception and integration in Sweden
content.description: The EU activated the Temporary Protection Directive after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine to rapidly provide protection for millions of people. The decision raises questions about how reception and integration work in practice, and the long-term consequences the directive may have for migration and societal development in Sweden.
content.extendedDescription:
When Russia invaded Ukraine, the EU activated the Temporary Protection Directive for the first time to rapidly provide protection for millions of people fleeing the war. The directive provided temporary residence permits, the right to work and access to education and healthcare in EU member states. At the same time, the reception of those fleeing has raised questions about how integration works in practice and the challenges and opportunities arising for both host countries and the people who have fled.

The event highlights experiences from the activation of the Temporary Protection Directive and discusses how reception and integration have worked in Sweden. The conversation also considers lessons for future crises and how policy, the labour market and society can help create better conditions for integration.

The programme takes the form of a conversation presenting different perspectives on migration and integration.

Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, millions of people have been forced to flee, and many have sought protection in northern Europe. Countries such as Sweden, Finland, Norway, Denmark and the Baltic states have received refugees in different ways, with varying systems for housing, work, education and social support. These differences raise questions about how reception and integration work in practice and which models provide the best conditions for people to establish themselves in a new society.

The event focuses on how Ukrainian refugees have been received in different northern European countries and the experience gained so far. The discussion highlights similarities and differences in policies, reception systems and integration measures, as well as lessons that may be important for future migration situations.

The programme takes the form of a conversation presenting different perspectives on reception and integration, drawing on research reports and practical experience.

content.title: From frontline to workforce: co-integration as Ukraine's competitive advantage
content.description: Ukraine is doing what no European country has done since 1945: reintegrating millions of civilians who became soldiers - teachers, engineers, farmers. Veteran unemployment exceeds 30%. The barrier is not skill - it is translation and trust. What does it take to build the bridge from both sides?
content.extendedDescription:
Once full demobilisation begins, Ukraine will have over 5 million veterans - up to 15% of the population. It is the only European country to have experienced full-scale war on its own soil since 1945, and the only one whose army consists substantially of mobilised civilians. Existing models were not built for this. 

This panel introduces co-integration: sustainable reintegration requires transformation on both sides - veterans learning to translate their experience, employers and institutions learning to recognise it. Reintegration asks veterans to adapt. Co-integration asks society to meet them halfway. 

Sweden has what Ukraine needs: inclusive labour market pathways, institutional infrastructure, experience supporting people outside the workforce. But knowledge runs both ways. content.title: Pharmacies of the future – how do we ensure pharmacy services throughout the country?
content.description: Pharmacies have a vital role, while the conditions for running pharmacies and providing pharmacy services across the country are becoming increasingly challenging. How can we maintain good access and make full use of pharmaceutical expertise?

Politicians from both political blocs say they want to develop pharmacies, but how will that happen? It is becoming harder to staff pharmacies from north to south with licensed pharmacists, which is a requirement for keeping a pharmacy open. Are remote pharmacists part of the solution? content.title: When everyone does their part but the system fails, children end up in crime
content.description: We know that 9 out of 10 children who commit crimes are already known to social services. How is it possible, despite all the interventions by schools, social services and others, that society cannot reverse the trend of ever more very young offenders?
content.extendedDescription:
Although many young people at risk of criminal involvement are well known to schools, social services and other actors, society is unable to change their trajectory. How is this possible when so many interventions are made – often over a long period? The seminar explores why today’s governance, financing and organisation mean that everyone does their part, but the system as a whole fails. We connect this to SustainGov’s focus area, the social contract of the future, and how a new model of joint action, outcome-based governance and shared investment could create real change in young people’s lives.

We discuss how society can move from silos to coherent systems where responsibility is shared, data is used wisely and resources are directed towards real outcomes, rather than just individual interventions. Can the new Social Services Act help build a new social contract around young people at risk of being drawn into crime?
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: The future of Ukrainian refugees – what happens after the Temporary Protection Directive?
content.description: The EU’s Temporary Protection Directive has given millions of Ukrainians temporary protection in Europe. But that protection is time-limited. What happens to Ukrainian refugees in Sweden when the directive ends? This raises discussions about return, integration and Sweden’s longer-term responsibility.
content.extendedDescription:
After Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the EU activated the Temporary Protection Directive to rapidly protect people fleeing the war. The directive has enabled millions of Ukrainians to live, work and study in different European countries. At the same time, the protection is temporary, raising questions about what happens when the directive eventually ends.

The event focuses on the future of Ukrainian refugees in Sweden. The discussion covers the possibility of returning to Ukraine, conditions for integration in the country and political decisions that may be needed in the future. Consequences for the labour market, education and societal development are also highlighted.

The programme takes the form of a conversation discussing different perspectives on migration, integration and Sweden’s responsibility.
content.subject: Integration/diversity

content.title: What do we need parents for? Trust, support and the way forward for parents in Sweden
content.description: Parenting is under pressure from growing mistrust, polarisation and distance between families and societal institutions. How do we build support that strengthens trust and reaches the parents who need it most? A conversation bringing research and practice together to understand what actually makes a difference for families today.
content.extendedDescription:
How is parenting in Sweden really doing? The social climate is becoming increasingly polarised, and many parents describe a growing sense of mistrust – both towards society and from its institutions. At the same time, professionals face a paradox: both scrutinising and supporting, both reporting concerns and building relationships.

In this conversation, we discuss how parenting support can better build trust, reach the right people and remain relevant. What do we know about which interventions work? How do we reach parents in areas where the distance between authorities and citizens is greatest? And how is support affected by the stereotypes and assumptions that shape today’s political debate?

We offer a warm conversation, important perspectives – and, of course, coffee and cake.

content.title: Four years of uncertainty – what happens now to Ukrainian refugees?
content.description: Europe and the Nordic countries are now entering the fifth year of the Temporary Protection Directive, which provides time-limited residence and work permits for Ukrainian refugees in the EU. A way out of this temporary solution must now be found – but how?
content.extendedDescription:
For four years, the Temporary Protection Directive has allowed decisions about what should happen to Ukrainians living in the Nordic countries if the war becomes prolonged to be postponed. But this year, the countries must develop new solutions. Although the directive is shared by all, national approaches in the Nordic region have differed and have been among the most varied in Europe.

• How has the Nordic experiment with the Temporary Protection Directive worked – what consequences have the different applications produced?
• What will the different Nordic approaches look like when the time-limited residence and work permits expire – will everyone have the same or different solutions?

The event presents new research on how Ukrainian refugees have fared in the Nordic region. Comparative analyses show that Sweden stands out. Updated analyses of policy developments will also be presented as a starting point for a discussion about what we have learned and what solutions we may see ahead.

content.title: Can we regulate our way to world-class performance? Rules, relationships and results in Swedish organisations
content.description: When customers come up against regulations, satisfaction drops sharply. What is intended to create security is instead experienced as suspicion, inflexibility and a lack of room to act. At the same time, society’s demands for compliance, documentation and supervision are growing. How can we increase the focus on creating value?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar summarises the past year’s studies of customer experience from Svenskt Kvalitetsindex. Together with guests, we analyse how customer relationships, governance and performance develop over time and what drives long-term competitiveness. This year’s theme is clear: rule-based management risks crowding out value creation.
In several of Sweden’s largest industries, the data shows the same pattern. When customers come up against regulations, satisfaction drops sharply. What is intended to create security is instead experienced as suspicion, inflexibility and a lack of room to act. At the same time, demands for compliance, documentation and supervision are growing.
The question is not whether we should have rules, but what happens when governance becomes more important than the solution.

content.title: How do we get new housing construction moving – and how much do we need to build?
content.description: The housing market is becoming increasingly divided. Vacancies are rising in some places, while shortages persist in others. Despite severe housing shortages in major cities and growing towns, it is difficult to make new construction financially viable.
content.extendedDescription:
Low levels of new construction combined with housing shortages lead to higher housing prices and staffing problems, as companies struggle to attract the right people because housing is hard to arrange. This in turn holds back growth. On a personal level, it becomes harder for young people to leave home – or move for studies or love – and starting a family is delayed.
What are the problems? Financing? Rent setting? Planning and building regulations? The situation and possible solutions are analysed and discussed from several perspectives, covering both rented and owner-occupied housing.
Together with several industry stakeholders, Bostadspolitik.se hosts the natural meeting place for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: The balance between performance and recovery – how do we maximise competitiveness?
content.description: Swedish productivity growth has weakened, and several key societal systems are struggling to deliver results. At the same time, growing rule-based management is hampering Swedish competitiveness. How can we strike a balance between governance, performance and recovery?
content.extendedDescription:
Svenskt Kvalitetsindex presents two national studies. Together, they provide a unique picture of the state of Swedish workplaces and what it means for performance. The pattern is clear. Employee satisfaction is relatively stable, but customer satisfaction is under pressure. Information sharing is inadequate, and uncertainty among employees is growing. We also see that many do not really know where their organisation is heading.
What happens to a team when its direction is unclear? Can people perform sustainably when anxiety and a lack of feedback affect everyday working life? And how does a team’s capability relate to customer experience and business results?
This seminar shares insights from work with high-performing teams in business and what we can learn from elite sport about clear goals, roles and learning. The question is not only how we feel at work, but what our working environment does to our capacity to perform and therefore to our customer relationships.
speakerTitles: Former Elite Cross-Country Skier, Project Manager

content.title: AI in practice – leading with digital capabilities
content.description: As AI-driven organisational development changes how organisations create value, it becomes a clear leadership issue. How do we transform processes, ways of working and financial management tools – and develop digital leadership that makes IT an investment in innovation and greater value for Sweden?

AI-driven organisational development is now changing how organisations lead, prioritise and create value. For Sweden to meet societal challenges and maintain its innovative strength, leaders need the courage to transform ways of working, processes and financial management tools. In both business and the public sector, IT is often seen as a cost to reduce, even though digital investment is crucial to realising value, developing new revenue streams and strengthening services for customers, citizens and employees.

content.title: When threats move closer to the individual – the role of close protection in a new security landscape
content.description: Threats against people in roles essential to society are increasing. Meanwhile, state close protection primarily covers national leaders. What role can private providers play?

Securitas is one of Sweden’s largest providers of protection for essential operations and part of the structure protecting many of the country’s valuable assets. content.title: How do we take responsibility for the labour market of the future?
content.description: AI is changing jobs. With the right skills, AI becomes an opportunity, not a threat. Sweden can take a leading role – but this requires investment in education, career transitions and inclusive technology education so that no one is left behind.
content.extendedDescription: AI will change many jobs: new roles are emerging and some tasks are disappearing. With the right skills development, AI is an opportunity, not a threat. Sweden is well placed thanks to the Swedish model and a strong tradition of career transitions and retraining. The government wants Sweden to be among the world’s ten leading AI nations and to lead Europe in public-sector AI. Achieving this requires both specialist expertise and broad skills: how do we prepare students for a labour market shaped by AI, how do we attract more women to AI and technology education, and who takes responsibility for implementation? If we invest in knowledge and AI leadership now, we can strengthen competitiveness and safeguard public services – but all parties must contribute so that no one is left behind.
content.subject: Digitalisation

content.title: Architecture in a new landscape – what do construction and property businesses expect from AI and architects?
content.description: AI is fundamentally changing how architecture is created, evaluated and delivered. The construction sector is advancing rapidly, and we are in the midst of a paradigm shift – but what does this actually mean for relationships between architects, contractors and property developers?
content.extendedDescription:
Property developers are already seeing AI open doors to new ways of working and expanded services. The question is no longer whether AI will change the industry, but how architects can use it as a value-creating tool to deliver more, better and smarter.

What do property developers and contractors expect from architectural services when AI handles more and more design work, early project stages and building permit processes? What new opportunities do they see, and what additional value can architectural services contribute? How do business models change when processes change? And how can AI strengthen collaboration in large, complex projects without compromising architectural quality?

content.title: A new management model for a new era – how do we lead organisations when complexity is the norm?
content.description: Organisations today operate in a world marked by uncertainty, rapid technological development, growing regulatory demands and constant transitions. Many management systems were designed for a time when stability, control and process maturity were sufficient. But what is required when change is a permanent condition?
content.extendedDescription: Organisations today operate in a world marked by uncertainty, rapid technological development, growing regulatory demands and constant transitions. At the same time, they are expected to deliver sustainable results, build trust and develop their operations over time. Many management systems were designed for a time when stability, control and process maturity were sufficient. But what is required when change is permanent? SIQ presents and discusses its work on a revised management model, developed to meet today’s demands for resilience, learning and professional judgement. What does the latest knowledge tell us about how organisations create long-term quality and sustainable results? How do we build structures that strengthen responsibility and adaptability without losing direction? And how do we ensure that governance supports development rather than hindering it?

content.title: How do we build resilience against hybrid threats?
content.description: Sweden faces growing hybrid threats in the shadow of the war in Ukraine. What does Russian hybrid warfare look like in practice? How vulnerable is Sweden to cyberattacks, sabotage and disinformation? And how can Swedish authorities and NATO strengthen our resilience?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a breakfast seminar, with coffee and rolls served from 08.15.

The seminar explores how Russia’s hybrid warfare affects Sweden and Europe through cyberattacks, sabotage, disinformation and infiltration. How vulnerable are our democratic processes? How are Sweden’s cooperation within NATO and its relationship with Ukraine affected? And how can Swedish authorities and allies strengthen our resilience against hybrid threats? Drawing on examples from our region, the discussion covers Russia’s hybrid capabilities, efforts to identify and attribute threats, and the measures needed to prevent and respond to influence operations against Sweden and our partner countries.

The seminar is part of Folk och Försvar’s arena in Almedalen – a meeting place for dialogue, knowledge sharing and cooperation on Sweden’s security. It brings together participants from across society to contribute to a safe, free and democratic Sweden.

content.title: The EU’s housing plan – how will, can and should Sweden respond?
content.description: The European Commission has presented its European Affordable Housing Plan, aiming to improve access to housing for households struggling to gain a foothold in the housing market. However, decisions on how to use these opportunities are made nationally and locally.
content.extendedDescription:
For Sweden, the plan raises several questions: Should it be used to strengthen efforts to tackle homelessness and financial hardship? Could it help improve financing solutions or create new models for cooperation? How do we ensure that European initiatives strengthen rather than undermine the conditions for long-term investment? Ultimately, is a universal or a targeted approach to housing the solution to the problems we face, and in which direction is the EU taking us?
Together with a number of industry participants, Bostadspolitik.se hosts the go-to arena for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Freedom from fossil fuels – the path to competitiveness and security of supply
content.description: Swedish businesses are ready to contribute to the energy transition while creating jobs and growth in Sweden. Political action is needed for a more resilient energy system in which fossil fuels have been phased out.
content.extendedDescription:
In recent years, geopolitical developments have repeatedly had major consequences for Europe’s energy supply and competitiveness as energy prices have soared. Our dependence on fossil fuels makes us vulnerable to events elsewhere in the world that we have no power to influence.
To withstand these crises, it is crucial to accelerate the phase-out of fossil fuels, improve efficiency, electrify and invest in fossil-free solutions for both industry and transport. It is therefore vital for Sweden and Europe to maintain their climate targets and the level of ambition in the key policy instruments that provide incentives to phase out fossil fuels and emissions. Transitioning away from fossil fuels is how we can eliminate the risks of price shocks in oil and gas markets and strengthen our own resilience and competitiveness.
Energiföretagen, Teknikföretagen and Hagainitiativet want political action for a more resilient energy system in which fossil fuels have been phased out.
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: Protect our water – smart water management and circular solutions create resource-efficient buildings
content.description: How do we create resource-efficient water solutions in a society where water is an increasingly strained resource?
content.extendedDescription:
During Almedalsveckan, we invite you to discuss two crucial perspectives: smart water use and circular construction. Using smart technology and connected mixer taps, we enable real-time measurement, control and optimisation of water flows – reducing both water and energy consumption. We also show how reducing new production, reusing products and using products made with circular materials improve resource efficiency in both new and existing buildings.

At our stand, you can meet experts in water issues, certification requirements, technical solutions and reuse. Refill your bottle at our water station and talk to us about how small choices can make a big difference. Under the motto “Protect our water”, we show concrete steps towards a more sustainable construction and property sector. Come and visit us!
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: The rental housing market – can we achieve a better balance?
content.description: The housing market has changed in recent years. While there is still a severe housing shortage in major cities, especially Stockholm, the picture is different elsewhere in Sweden. Some smaller municipalities have high vacancy rates, a problem also found in several growing towns and cities.
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, we analyse the different market conditions for rental properties. We then discuss the situation from market and policy perspectives: can we create a balanced rental housing market? Two panels:
1. The role of rental housing in growth – can people move to where the jobs are today?
The housing shortage in major cities – particularly Stockholm – threatens growth, as businesses cannot attract the right skills when housing is unavailable. This also affects occupations essential to society. How should the situation be addressed?
2. The new challenges – how do we tackle them?
Regional cities are now seeing rising vacancy rates. In rural areas, demolition is being discussed. Meanwhile, in some places rental homes are disappearing through conversion to tenant-owned housing. What role should rental housing play, and how can it become more attractive?
Together with a number of industry participants, Bostadspolitik.se hosts the go-to arena for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Children’s physical activity and motor skills – a growing public health problem
content.description: More and more children get too little physical activity, affecting their health, motor skills and school performance. Insufficient physical activity is a growing public health problem that risks causing enormous health problems in the future.
content.extendedDescription:
Children are becoming less physically active, while increasing numbers show poor motor skills. Research shows that the foundations for movement and motor skills are laid early in life – and that shortcomings in the first few years can have consequences for health, learning and quality of life far into the future.

This seminar focuses on children’s physical activity and motor development as an urgent and growing public health issue. What is the state of children’s health, and what explains it? Why are we not reaching enough children – particularly in the crucial early years? Do parents lack knowledge? What responsibilities do schools, community organisations and politicians have? What do we need to do to reverse the trend?

Drawing on research and practical experience, participants from different sectors discuss how to create more accessible, inclusive and enjoyable environments for play and physical activity, and how we can strengthen both our children’s motor skills and their health.

content.title: Rules, registers or results – what can Sweden learn from Denmark?
content.description: Requirements, checks and registers concerning civil society have increased sharply in recent years. After a period in which numerous requirements and checks have been introduced, the government and civil society need to evaluate them together. Effective measures that prevent the misuse of taxpayers’ money should continue and be developed.
content.extendedDescription:
In Denmark, the government and civil society have joined forces in a joint process to simplify regulations. Which bureaucratic obstacles facing civil society fail to deliver benefits proportionate to the effort involved? In the Danish government’s own words: “The government wants to tackle the unnecessary bureaucracy that creates difficulties for dedicated volunteers in the country’s associations.”

It is a matter of finding a balance. Government grants must go to the activities they are intended for and must not be misused. But government grants and voluntary efforts must not be wasted on red tape and unnecessary bureaucracy either. Inspired by Denmark, Studieförbunden proposes that the government and civil society jointly review the administrative requirements imposed on civil society, with the aim of simplifying them and freeing up resources for core activities.

Which measures are effective? What problems do they solve, and at what cost? Effective measures that prevent the misuse of taxpayers’ money should be developed. Checks that cost more than they are worth should be removed.

content.title: OSA turns 10 – why is preventive work more important than ever?
content.description: The regulations on the organisational and social work environment (OSA) have given us better conditions for working systematically and successfully on the work environment. How do we now step up preventive efforts to make tomorrow’s workplaces fit for the future?
content.extendedDescription:
This year marks ten years since the regulations on the organisational and social work environment (OSA) came into force. They have given employers and employees a shared language and clearer tools for issues such as workloads and victimisation. Despite this, stress-related ill health remains a major challenge, and many people do not know how to carry out this work in practice.

Arbetsmiljöverket reflects on the effects of the regulations, and Magnus Åkerström presents challenges in their application. Prevent shows how workplaces move from theory to action, with tools for identifying risks before they lead to ill health. Suntarbetsliv shares experiences from organisations that have linked their OSA work to regular management processes – and highlights why frontline managers are key.

Kajsa Rosén, Strategirådet, discusses societal benefits and impact measurement – what is needed for work environment policies to make a real difference? A concluding panel with the social partners discusses how we take the next step.

content.title: How do we make work environment efforts as effective as possible?
content.description: Many work environment challenges exist at an organisational level, but interventions often target individuals. How can we shift the perspective so that measures are taken where they make the greatest difference? And which ways of working have a real impact?
content.extendedDescription:
Heavy workloads are a challenge in many workplaces, affecting both employees’ health and organisational productivity. Regulations are in place, but managers often feel that their efforts do not have the intended effect. New research shows why: willingness is not lacking, but the necessary conditions are. For work environment efforts to have a real impact, senior managers need to ensure that these issues are prioritised, that there is a shared understanding at every level of the organisation, and that sufficient resources are available to put intentions into practice.

Magnus Åkerström, Research Leader at Institutet för stressmedicin ISM, presents findings from a highly topical research project that describes, in three steps, what successful work environment efforts require. As a participant, you will have a unique opportunity to explore this and reflect on your own work environment efforts together with others.

content.title: Sweden in NATO – military build-up and responsibility
content.description: Sweden is rapidly expanding its military capabilities following NATO membership in 2024. What does the expansion of Sweden’s armed forces mean for Sweden’s security and military capability? What role is Sweden expected to take within NATO?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to Folk och Försvar’s “In conversation with” – a shorter, in-depth discussion with an invited guest about current issues in Swedish defence, foreign and security policy.

content.title: How does our view of children shape Sweden’s future?
content.description: How society treats children shapes both individuals and the future. Yet decisions about their circumstances and future often lack a shared view of children as holders of rights, potential and hope. What does it take to give more children the chance to succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
The connection is strong: how we see children influences the decisions we make, and those decisions in turn shape children’s everyday lives, opportunities and confidence in the future. All too often, children encounter low expectations rather than faith in their abilities and potential, and this is reflected in how we prioritise, organise and cooperate.

Our view of children needs to inform the whole chain, from overarching decisions to everyday encounters. A shared view of children is not only a matter of values, but of how schools, social services, civil society and leisure activities together create the conditions for children to grow.

When adults meet children with genuine commitment and faith in their abilities, the conditions change – for the child, for the group and for society as a whole.

The seminar brings together voices from schools, social services, civil society and student organisations for a discussion about what a shared view of children can mean in practice.

content.title: New drugs outpace the law – time to classify entire families of substances?
content.description: New synthetic drugs emerge faster than they can be banned. Small chemical changes allow substances to be sold legally until they are classified. Several countries have introduced generic classification to curb this trend. Should Sweden do the same?
content.extendedDescription:
The market for new psychoactive substances is changing rapidly. Small chemical modifications can produce new variants of known drugs that temporarily fall outside narcotics legislation. As a result, new cannabinoids, stimulants and opioids can be sold openly in shops and online until they have been investigated and classified. When a substance is banned, it is often quickly replaced by a new, similar variant. This phenomenon can currently be seen with synthetic cannabinoids, among others, and was previously seen with fentanyl analogues. These developments mean that legislation and authorities are often one step behind.
In Sweden, Folkhälsomyndigheten investigates new substances and submits classification proposals to the government. In the meantime, the products can continue to be sold. Several European countries, including Norway and Denmark, have introduced what is known as generic classification, under which entire groups of chemically similar substances can be banned at the same time. The seminar discusses whether such a model could also work in Sweden.

content.title: How do we create healthy working lives and safe workplaces?
content.description: With working life changing rapidly and pressure growing on both managers and employees, new ways are needed to create sustainable workplaces founded on collective agreements. Can effective preventive work, civil behaviour, psychological safety and AI strengthen the work environment?
content.extendedDescription:
We offer breakfast while presenting a taste of our full day of knowledge and inspiration from researchers, the social partners and Afa Försäkring’s experts. Afa Fastigheter presents the seminar “The office, culture and architecture” – on how physical design and organisational culture together create attractive and sustainable work environments.

content.title: State organ theft – a crime against humanity
content.description: 25 years ago, state hospitals, secretly cooperating with the police, prisons and military, began systematically stealing organs on a large scale from illegally imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners. Today, other groups are also affected, and it has emerged that children are being kidnapped too. What can Sweden do about this?
content.extendedDescription: Recently, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has extended its persecution abroad as well. It ensures that foreign media spread propaganda on its behalf. It also tries to sabotage activities organised by Falun Gong practitioners, for example through false bomb threats. How can these attacks be stopped? Since 2006, reports have emerged of organ harvesting in hospitals in China, with Falun Gong practitioners as the main victims. This has been verified by doctors and witnesses. An EU resolution from January 2024 calls on all EU countries to take immediate measures to condemn state-sanctioned organ harvesting. Will Sweden follow other countries’ example and introduce laws that prevent Swedish citizens from travelling to China for organ transplants and unwittingly contributing to this crime? We hear witnesses’ and victims’ own accounts of the brutal persecution in China. One of Europe’s leading experts on China shares his view of the current situation in China and why it concerns us too.

content.title: Macroeconomic analysis – where is the world heading and how does it affect Sweden’s housing market?
content.description: Geopolitical unrest in several regions, brutal wars. The world in 2026 is nowhere near as stable as most of us would wish. We read about oil price shocks and tariff threats, and have world leaders who are, to put it mildly, hard to read.
content.extendedDescription:
Wars and unrest around the world naturally also have a major impact on the national economy, and general uncertainty leads to caution in the housing market – both in consumers’ willingness to make the biggest investment of their lives and in housing developers’ willingness to start new projects. What does the macroeconomic situation mean for Sweden’s housing market? What is the outlook for interest rates? Which macroeconomic events really matter, and what can we dismiss as noise? Robert Boije, one of the country’s most respected economists, shares his view of the world, Sweden and the housing market today, and also discusses his conclusions with Daniel Waldenström, Professor of Economics.
Together with a number of industry participants, Bostadspolitik.se hosts the go-to arena for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Games in everyday life, science and the wider world
content.description: For thousands of years, games have been a popular form of entertainment and an integral part of our social and cultural interactions. Today, some of the world’s best games are made in Sweden, and 6.9 million Swedes play video games. What do you know about games, gaming culture, game development and Sweden’s gaming success story?
content.extendedDescription:
SpelAlmedalen is a meeting place that puts games in the spotlight in Almedalen. Learn more about games as a form of expression, culture, an industry and a field of research!

Here you can see an exhibition about Sweden’s gaming success story, try games made by local students, play board games and meet people from different parts of Sweden’s gaming community.

The SpelAlmedalen programme has been developed in cooperation between Uppsala Universitet, Svenska Spelforskarrådet, Sverok and Dataspelsbranschen. Together, we want to share knowledge about games as an industry, a cultural activity and a field of research, develop cooperation and invite discussion about what future gaming policy should look like.

Visit SpelAlmedalen at Uppsala Universitet’s Department of Game Design at Strandgatan 1 in Visby, Tuesday–Thursday during Almedalsveckan. Read more at spelalmedalen.se!

content.title: Psychological safety – how does it strengthen safety and trust at work?
content.description: Psychological safety strengthens safety, trust and learning. When people feel able to raise risks early, accidents and ill health can be prevented while quality and productivity improve. How can managers build and strengthen this sense of safety in the organisation’s everyday work to achieve sustainable long-term results?
content.extendedDescription:
When employees feel able to speak openly, ask questions and report incidents without fear, learning and cooperation improve and the risk of accidents and ill health decreases. Research shows that teams with high psychological safety report risks earlier and learn more quickly from incidents. When psychological safety is low, problems risk remaining invisible and safety efforts are weakened.

Christina Björklund, a researcher at Karolinska Institutet, presents the latest research, funded by Afa Försäkring, on the relationship between psychological safety and the risk of accidents, stress and ill health.

Prevent and Suntarbetsliv share experiences of how organisations work in practice. Together with Sveriges Företagshälsor, Industriarbetsgivarna and LO, we discuss how organisations that take psychological safety seriously also create sustainable and successful workplaces over the long term.

content.title: Could AI be the key to healthy working lives?
content.description: AI is changing work and opening up new opportunities to improve the work environment. The technology can help us detect risks earlier, provide better information for decisions and free up time for human interaction and cooperation. How can AI be used to improve the work environment without creating new risks?
content.extendedDescription:
AI is often described as the key to more efficient organisations, but the technology also changes how work is organised and managed – directly affecting the work environment. This seminar shifts the focus from technology to working life: what does it take for AI to contribute to healthy and sustainable working lives in practice? And what responsibilities must employers, trade unions and leaders take on to steer developments in the right direction?

Mathias Collén, CEO of Afa Försäkring, describes the organisation’s AI journey. Per Långsved, Head of Sweden at Nordea, shares experiences from an organisation investing ambitiously in AI – and which has openly stated that the technology will radically affect its operations.

Hanna Birath, Akavia, explores what these developments mean for graduate professionals; Carola Löfstrand, LO, reflects on how the work environment is affected; and Suntarbetsliv shows how AI can be integrated into systematic work environment management. You will also see the winning entry from the “Hackathon for healthy working lives”.

content.title: State organ theft – a crime against humanity
content.description: 25 years ago, state hospitals, secretly cooperating with the police, prisons and military, began systematically stealing organs on a large scale from illegally imprisoned Falun Gong practitioners. Today, other groups are also affected, and it has emerged that children are being kidnapped too. What can Sweden do about this?
content.extendedDescription: Recently, the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) has extended its persecution abroad as well. It ensures that foreign media spread propaganda on its behalf. It also tries to sabotage activities organised by Falun Gong practitioners, for example through false bomb threats. How can these attacks be stopped? Since 2006, reports have emerged of organ harvesting in hospitals in China, with Falun Gong practitioners as the main victims. This has been verified by doctors and witnesses. An EU resolution from January 2024 calls on all EU countries to take immediate measures to condemn state-sanctioned organ harvesting. Will Sweden follow other countries’ example and introduce laws that prevent Swedish citizens from travelling to China for organ transplants and unwittingly contributing to this crime? We hear witnesses’ and victims’ own accounts of the brutal persecution in China. One of Europe’s leading experts on China shares his view of the current situation in China and why it concerns us too.

content.title: Social sustainability for housing companies: how do we know we are investing in the right things before investing more?
content.description: Social sustainability is becoming an increasingly natural part of Swedish housing companies’ work – but there are many different approaches, and companies find it difficult to prioritise and connect this work to business decisions and financing. What are the advantages and disadvantages of a shared industry practice – and what might it look like?
content.extendedDescription:
This seminar explores how to develop a more structured approach to social sustainability that is closely integrated with business: an approach that helps housing companies set the right priorities, create real benefits for society and also support management, valuation and sustainable financing. How do we know we are investing in the right things before investing more? Drawing on experience from tools and pilots already tested in the industry – for mapping, prioritisation, theories of change and follow-up – we discuss what could become the building blocks of a future industry methodology. The seminar invites businesses, politicians, finance and civil society into a shared discussion about how social sustainability work can move from ambition to common practice.
Together with a number of industry participants, Bostadspolitik.se hosts the go-to arena for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Taking greater responsibility for our own security
content.description: Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine has shaken the European security order, while uncertainty about the United States’ long-term commitment to Europe’s security has deepened the discussion about the need for greater European responsibility.
content.extendedDescription: How can the need for transatlantic cohesion be balanced with the demand for European strategic autonomy? And how can Sweden and Finland play a leading role in this transition?

content.title: Preparedness in a crisis – what lessons can be learned from the war in Ukraine?
content.description: The war in Ukraine shows the importance of strong civil and military preparedness. Society’s ability to protect the population, maintain essential services and manage crises is being tested. What lessons can other countries learn to strengthen their own preparedness?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has clearly demonstrated how crucial preparedness is to a society’s resilience. When a crisis strikes, essential services such as healthcare, energy, transport, communications and food supply must continue to function while the population’s safety is protected.

The event explores the lessons that can be learned from Ukraine’s handling of the war and how they can help develop preparedness in other countries. The discussion addresses civil preparedness, cooperation between authorities, businesses and civil society, and how societies can prepare for complex crises.

The programme takes the form of a conversation exploring different perspectives on preparedness and societal resilience.

content.title: What is the property sector’s role if or when the enemy comes?
content.description: The geopolitical situation and Sweden’s security situation have deteriorated dramatically over the past decade. We see recurring GPS interference in the Baltic Sea, airspace is regularly violated and the shadow fleet sails around our country. Society needs to focus more on resilience, safety and security.
content.extendedDescription:
Many different actors face new demands – demands we did not want but must meet. The property sector is one of the most important actors in creating a safer, more stable and more resilient society. What can and should the industry do to take responsibility? What incentives need to be introduced to ensure that measures are implemented? Are we ready if/when the enemy comes?
Together with a number of industry participants, Bostadspolitik.se hosts the go-to arena for housing policy in Almedalen – at Clarion Hotel Wisby (Paviljongen) on Tuesday and Wednesday.

content.title: Twinning partnerships between Swedish municipalities, regions and Ukrainian cities – how do they work?
content.description: Cooperation between Swedish municipalities and Ukrainian cities has become increasingly important during the war. Twinning partnerships enable knowledge, resources and experience to be shared. How can these partnerships provide support during the war and contribute to Ukraine’s long-term reconstruction?
content.extendedDescription:
Twinning partnerships between municipalities have long been a way to strengthen international relations, exchange experience and develop local cooperation. Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine, many Swedish municipalities have deepened or initiated partnerships with Ukrainian cities to provide support, knowledge and practical solutions in a difficult situation.

The event explores the role that municipal partnerships can play in times of crisis. Through cooperation, municipalities can share experience in areas such as education, spatial planning, crisis preparedness and public administration. These relationships can also contribute to Ukraine’s long-term reconstruction and strengthen democratic institutions at the local level.

The programme takes the form of a conversation exploring different perspectives on twinning partnerships and international municipal cooperation.

content.title: Why does the Chinese regime want to eliminate Falun Gong/Falun Dafa?
content.description: Falun Dafa’s principles of Truthfulness, Compassion and Forbearance are incompatible with the Chinese Communist Party’s ideology, which is why the practice remains persecuted in China today. Practitioners in China have made enormous sacrifices to expose the persecution of principles that we in the West celebrate. But what are we in the West doing?
content.extendedDescription: The persecution of Falun Gong practitioners has continued since 1999 while the outside world has remained relatively silent. Why does the international community not react when severe persecution takes place openly, including the theft of organs from prisoners of conscience who all die in the process? How is this persecution spreading beyond China? How does the persecution concern us in Sweden? Does it pose any security risks here? Questions that concern us include which goods are manufactured in labour camps where Falun Gong practitioners and other dissidents are detained. Should Sweden’s relationship with China be reassessed in light of the human rights violations committed there? China expert Manyan Ng addresses the subject daily at 15.30-16.15. Falun Gong is demonstrated every day at 9-18. You are welcome to try the exercises.

content.title: Sweden’s support for Ukraine – what role does aid play?
content.description: Sweden provides extensive support to Ukraine through humanitarian aid, development cooperation and reconstruction efforts. This also raises questions about how the support can be effective, sustained over the long term and contribute to a resilient and democratic Ukraine.
content.extendedDescription:
Since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Sweden has increased its support to the country through humanitarian aid, financial measures and long-term development cooperation. This includes assistance for people in urgent need, support for essential services and efforts to strengthen democracy, institutions and reconstruction.

The event highlights the role of Swedish aid in supporting Ukraine and how these efforts can contribute both during the ongoing war and to future reconstruction. The discussion considers how international aid can strengthen societal resilience, support reforms and create the conditions for long-term development.

The programme takes the form of a conversation exploring different perspectives on aid, international cooperation and Ukraine’s future.

content.title: Fuel choices that will shape European shipping for decades – is policy steering in the right direction?
content.description: Shipping must make the transition – but which fuel should power the vessels of the future? Many current policy initiatives point to new alternatives such as electrofuels, biofuels, hydrogen and ammonia. Yet major questions remain about production, safety, energy needs and infrastructure.
content.extendedDescription:
Decisions made today about support, regulations and incentives risk steering investment in a particular direction long before it is clear which solutions are actually scalable and feasible. For shipping, these investments need to work for 25–30 years. The choices affect not only shipping companies but also energy systems, port infrastructure and industrial competitiveness in Sweden and northern Europe.

How do we ensure that policy creates the right conditions for a transition that both reduces emissions and is technically and economically feasible?

This seminar brings together representatives from shipping, the energy sector, politics and public authorities to discuss which decisions are needed now – and how we avoid locking shipping into fuel solutions that are not yet ready.

The seminar is moderated by Per Tunell, VP Sustainability & Business Development.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: From words to action – robust logistics for total defence in the Nordic and Baltic regions
content.description: The deteriorating security situation in Europe has highlighted the need for robust total defence. For Sweden to provide and receive host nation support, functioning logistics chains, transport capacity and robust supply flows are essential. Shipping plays an important role. But are today’s structures sufficient?
content.extendedDescription:
Logistics does not end at the quay. Effective onward connections to rail and road are needed to keep goods moving – a robust intermodal system that can handle large volumes under time pressure and connect Sweden, the Nordic region and the Baltic states.

How do we strengthen the role of shipping, ports and civilian logistics services in total defence? How do we ensure that capacity, expertise and resources are available where and when they are needed? And what investments, partnerships and decisions are required to build more resilient Nordic–Baltic logistics and resource supply?

The seminar brings together politicians and businesses, with representatives from Sweden, Finland and Norway, to discuss how transport, port and logistics systems can be strengthened in a new security situation. Finland and Norway have extensive experience of total defence and civil–military cooperation, but different models and priorities. What lessons can Sweden learn – and how do we move from words to action?

Michael Kellermann moderates.
speakerTitles: Head of Security and Defence Policy
National Adviser on Public–Private Cooperation in Total Defence

content.title: Heta stubben: does Moderaterna want a national boost to outdoor recreation after the election?
content.description: Outdoor recreation is good for health and well-being – 94 per cent of Swedes agree. Outdoor activities and accessible nature counteract sedentary lifestyles, loneliness and ill health. Yet the potential of outdoor recreation to strengthen public health and preparedness is underused. Which parties are campaigning for a major boost to outdoor recreation?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year’s Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of boiled coffee from the outdoor stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will hold conversations with party leaders and other decision-makers on various occasions about their vision for outdoor recreation. How can outdoor recreation and nature activities have as natural a place in politics as they do in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be physically active in nature? How can outdoor recreation help strengthen preparedness?

Four out of five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have fitness levels so poor that they put their health at risk. Sedentary lifestyles and mental ill health cost society five per cent of GDP. This is deeply problematic for individuals, public health and Swedes’ resilience in crises. At the same time, we know that investment in physical activity is highly profitable.

The upkeep of our nature reserves and national parks is severely neglected, even though we know that spending time in attractive natural surroundings benefits our physical and mental health.

content.title: Adult education at the election – what do politicians want for study associations?
content.description: Non-formal adult education faces historic changes and tough financial choices. But what is the long-term political vision? Are study associations a tool for integration, a driving force for cultural life or a democratic infrastructure expected to fend for itself? Clear answers are needed now.
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a discussion about visions, choices and the place of non-formal adult education in building Swedish society. Under the heading “Adult education at the election”, we invite representatives of parliamentary parties on the Committee on Cultural Affairs to reflect on the future of study associations. Instead of short-term debating points, we seek long-term solutions and the ideological foundations of tomorrow’s adult education policy.

Building on this spring’s webinar series “Studieförbunden möter”, we explore the opportunities and challenges facing study associations in greater depth. Politicians from the eight parties explain how they view the role of study associations as democratic infrastructure and a force for learning.

The seminar takes place at Civilsamhällesarenan. We begin with short extracts from this spring’s online meetings to set the scene, followed by a conversation focused on constructive proposals and ideological clarity. The audience will have the opportunity to hear a broad political panel discuss the future direction of non-formal adult education.

content.title: From bureaucracy to a calm learning environment: how relational leadership and innovation improve learning outcomes
content.description: In a school system marked by increasing political micromanagement and an approach leaning more towards rules than warmth, new ways of achieving the goals are needed. How do relational leadership and proven methods create a school where both students and teachers can succeed?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish schools face a paradox: the focus on safety and a calm learning environment has never been greater, while their mission is weighed down by increasing bureaucracy and administrative requirements. How do we navigate this landscape without losing sight of students’ learning and the human aspects of education?
The seminar presents how innovative ways of working can break the deadlock. We explore concrete examples of creating safety, a calm learning environment and improved learning through Elmemodellen. By combining a relational approach among staff with inclusive learning environments, we show that results can improve even under complex conditions.
Key questions:

content.title: Heta stubben: does Sverigedemokraterna want a national boost to outdoor recreation after the election?
content.description: Outdoor recreation is good for health and well-being – 94 per cent of Swedes agree. Outdoor activities and accessible nature counteract sedentary lifestyles, loneliness and ill health. Yet the potential of outdoor recreation to strengthen public health and preparedness is underused. Which parties are campaigning for a major boost to outdoor recreation?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year’s Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of boiled coffee from the outdoor stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will hold conversations with party leaders and other decision-makers on various occasions about their vision for outdoor recreation. How can outdoor recreation and nature activities have as natural a place in politics as they do in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be physically active in nature? How can outdoor recreation help strengthen preparedness?

Four out of five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have fitness levels so poor that they put their health at risk. Sedentary lifestyles and mental ill health cost society five per cent of GDP. This is deeply problematic for individuals, public health and Swedes’ resilience in crises. At the same time, we know that investment in physical activity is highly profitable.

The upkeep of our nature reserves and national parks is severely neglected, even though we know that spending time in attractive natural surroundings benefits our physical and mental health.

content.title: Do we need to know who lives in the apartment?
content.description: On 1 July, the opportunities to sublet tenant-owned apartments will expand.
