content.title: What is myth and what is fact when it comes to AI and energy?
content.description: Does the growing use of AI increase carbon emissions, or could AI actually be a tool for a sustainable energy transition? We often see conflicting claims about AI, energy use and data centres. But what is actually true, what is oversimplified, and what lacks clear answers?
content.extendedDescription:
What is actually true and false about AI’s impact on energy consumption and the environment?
- Is AI’s energy demand a climate risk?
- Is AI about to cause a global energy crisis?
- Can AI have a positive impact on the climate?
- Does AI drive up electricity prices?
- Can the AI boom strengthen Sweden’s competitiveness?

In this session, we untangle common myths and facts about AI’s impact on energy use and the environment. We discuss what actually drives AI’s energy demand, why context such as the energy mix and how AI is used matters greatly, and how greater transparency can support more informed decisions. The aim is to contribute to a more nuanced, fact-based discussion of AI’s role in the energy system and its climate impact.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: Skills and growth – what can we learn from Ireland?
content.description: Skills are crucial to growth, but how do we create the right conditions? In a few decades, Ireland has gone from crisis to one of Europe’s most dynamic economies. Modern skills and staffing solutions are key. What can Sweden learn?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to a breakfast seminar about skills, the labour market and growth.

Ireland is increasingly highlighted as a European example of how reforms, investments and skills provision can contribute to stronger growth. Meanwhile, Sweden faces major challenges involving skills shortages, weak productivity growth and a need for more investment.

What factors lie behind Ireland’s development, and what lessons could be relevant to Sweden? How can staffing and recruitment companies, businesses and politicians work together to strengthen growth? What role does businesses’ ability to find the right skills at the right time play?

Drawing on a new report, we bring together representatives from politics, business and the labour market for a conversation about Sweden’s competitiveness and future growth. The seminar begins with a short presentation of the report’s main conclusions, followed by a panel discussion with opportunities for audience questions.

content.title: Do we want to lead or follow? What kind of Sweden are we building?
content.description: AI is a tool to master, rather than a threat to fear. If Sweden acts now, we can steer developments towards growth, new jobs and better public services, in line with our values. The question is what kind of Sweden we want: a leading nation of innovation, or one that falls behind.
content.extendedDescription: AI is a tool we must master, rather than a threat we should fear. If Sweden acts now, we can shape AI in a way that promotes growth, new jobs, better public services and sustainable development – all in line with our democratic values. Instead of worrying about whether AI will take over, we should ask what we want the change to look like and what is needed to make it happen. Ultimately, this is about the kind of Sweden we want to live in: a country that drives innovation to become a world-leading, secure and sustainable welfare nation – or a country that passively lets others take the lead. We have the knowledge, the values and the experience of navigating major transitions together. If we seize the opportunities AI offers, Sweden can not only defend its position, but excel as a nation of innovation that improves people’s lives and creates the jobs of the future.

content.title: Heta stubben: Will Vänsterpartiet launch a national initiative to boost outdoor recreation after the election?
content.description: Outdoor recreation is good for health and well-being – 94 per cent of Swedes agree. Outdoor activities and accessible nature counteract sedentary lifestyles, loneliness and ill health. Yet the potential of outdoor recreation to strengthen public health and preparedness is underused. Which parties are campaigning for a major boost to outdoor recreation?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year’s Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of boiled coffee from the outdoor stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will hold conversations with party leaders and other decision-makers on various occasions about their vision for outdoor recreation. How can outdoor recreation and nature have as natural a place in politics as they do in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be physically active in nature?

Four out of five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have fitness levels so poor that they put their health at risk. Sedentary lifestyles and mental ill health cost society five per cent of GDP. This is deeply problematic for individuals, public health and Swedes’ resilience in crises. At the same time, we know that investment in physical activity is highly profitable.

The upkeep of our nature reserves and national parks is severely neglected, even though we know that spending time in attractive natural surroundings benefits our physical and mental health. Access to shores under the right of public access is under pressure.

content.title: Generation of contrasts: Greta versus Bianca
content.description: Opposites meet in Generation Z. How can it become easier for young people to shift towards more sustainable consumption? The green transition in an unstable world requires decision-makers with their feet on the ground and their eyes on the future.
content.extendedDescription:
Generation Z is full of paradoxes, with Greta and Bianca side by side. Every trend has a countertrend. Global solidarity meets more conservative individualism. Sales of second-hand clothing are rising, while throwaway shopping is just a click away.
Environmental and climate issues do not rank as highly on young people’s list of important societal issues. The climate crisis, the crisis facing nature and emissions of hazardous substances threaten the planet’s survival and our way of life. So the transition is urgent. Who bears responsibility? What opportunities lie in the green transition and a more circular economy? Who can we trust in an age of greenwashing?
A discussion between the young decision-makers of the future. Insights from Svanen, which has guided consumers towards more sustainable consumption since the ecolabel was established by Nordiska ministerrådet in 1989.

content.title: From import dependence to energy independence – concrete measures for aviation’s transition
content.description: To meet climate targets, strengthen competitiveness and secure access to strategically important aviation fuels, Sweden needs to act now. What concrete measures are needed for Sweden to take a leading role in aviation’s transition?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden faces a strategic choice. We can either remain dependent on imported fossil aviation fuels – for both civil aviation and Försvarsmakten – or build domestic production of sustainable aviation fuels. Such an investment would benefit the climate, industry and Sweden’s security of supply.
The prerequisites are in place. Sweden has access to sustainable biomass, competitively priced fossil-free electricity and world-class industrial expertise. What is missing is a clear, long-term policy framework that enables investment decisions in first-of-a-kind projects.
To meet climate targets, strengthen competitiveness and secure access to strategically important aviation fuels, the government needs to act promptly. In this seminar, we discuss concrete measures for Sweden to take a leading role in aviation’s transition.
speakerTitles: State Secretary at Landsbygds- och infrastrukturdepartementet

content.title: Heta stubben: Will Liberalerna launch a national initiative to boost outdoor recreation after the election?
content.description: Outdoor recreation is good for health and well-being – 94 per cent of Swedes agree. Outdoor activities and accessible nature counteract sedentary lifestyles, loneliness and ill health. Yet the potential of outdoor recreation to strengthen public health and preparedness is underused. Which parties are campaigning for a major boost to outdoor recreation?
content.extendedDescription:
Last year’s Almedalen success, Heta stubben, is back. With the sea as a backdrop and the aroma of boiled coffee from the outdoor stove, Friluftsfrämjandet will hold conversations with party leaders and other decision-makers on various occasions about their vision for outdoor recreation. How can outdoor recreation and nature activities have as natural a place in politics as they do in our hearts? How can more people be encouraged to be physically active in nature? How can outdoor recreation help strengthen preparedness?

Four out of five children get too little physical activity, and half of adults have fitness levels so poor that they put their health at risk. Sedentary lifestyles and mental ill health cost society five per cent of GDP. This is deeply problematic for individuals, public health and Swedes’ resilience in crises. At the same time, we know that investment in physical activity is highly profitable.

The upkeep of our nature reserves and national parks is severely neglected, even though we know that spending time in attractive natural surroundings benefits our physical and mental health.
speakerTitles: Deputy Chair of the parliamentary Committee on Cultural Affairs

content.title: From crisis to strength: a sustainable healthcare workforce through modern workplaces
content.description: Securing the future of healthcare requires a sustainable working environment in which nurses are able and choose to stay, grow and contribute. Motivation in everyday work is crucial, and digitalisation is one of several areas that must provide support that frees up time and strengthens quality in day-to-day healthcare.
content.extendedDescription:
How do we create modern workplaces in person-centred healthcare where nurses choose to stay, develop and contribute? This question is central to the university hospitals within the Swedish University Hospital Alliance (SUHA) – and relevant to the whole healthcare system.
In this discussion, we highlight what current research shows about motivation in nurses’ everyday work and how these insights can be put into practice at different levels. Together with you as a participant, we explore factors that affect the working environment and workforce provision, with digitalisation as an important element – an opportunity to improve quality and free up time, but also a potential pitfall in a pressured working day. You are welcome to contribute actively with ideas, experience and suggestions on how we can work together to create more sustainable, modern and attractive healthcare workplaces, focusing on future opportunities. The discussion also aims to lay the groundwork for continued dialogue in other forums.

content.title: Books and games – rivals or friends?
content.description: Why are games this year’s theme at major literary events? Games are stories, language and creativity – from digital adventures to board games. They challenge the imagination and create new ways to experience stories. How can games foster a love of reading, develop language and inspire writing?
content.extendedDescription:
In 2026, games are the theme of both Bokmässan and Läslovet. Why?
The panel discusses how games can be used as a tool for storytelling, how they can develop language and inspire reading and writing, and why it is important to include games in public debate. How can we use games’ potential to reach new audiences and create new forms of literary experience? And how can we encourage collaboration between the games industry, schools and cultural life? Drawing on both digital games and traditional board and role-playing games, we explore how games can enrich our understanding of storytelling and language.

content.title: Democracy needs free voices – but who funds them?
content.description: As parts of civil society face reduced public funding and fierce competition for members and donors, other forms of funding become crucial. But which are sustainable, and which risk making civil society dependent on commercial or political interests?
content.extendedDescription:
Democracy rests on people and organisations that can act freely, make their voices heard and scrutinise those in power. Civil society is expected to take increasing responsibility for addressing social challenges, strengthening cohesion and defending democratic values. At the same time, many organisations are under pressure from falling membership income, less predictable grant systems and tougher competition for people’s engagement.
Which forms of funding strengthen an independent and vibrant civil society, and which risk creating dependencies? What role do public-benefit lotteries play in securing long-term conditions for non-profit organisations? And how does a strong civil society relate to the need for free and independent media?
TV4, Postkodlotteriet and Svalo bring together representatives from the media, civil society and the mission-driven non-profit sector for a discussion about democracy’s infrastructure, the importance of independent funding and what is needed for more voices to continue making a difference in society.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: New and old arenas for recruitment into criminal networks
content.description: Recruitment into criminal networks is a major societal problem affecting young people in Sweden. What do the findings of two research studies show: one focusing on open drug scenes, and one on how children are drawn into criminal networks through school?
content.extendedDescription: In recent years, considerable attention has focused on recruitment through the internet and social media into criminal networks and to commit serious acts of violence. These recruitment arenas have complemented – and partly replaced – older arenas for recruitment into criminal networks. At the same time, more traditional socialisation and recruitment into criminal networks continue, including in disadvantaged areas, around open drug scenes and in schools, according to current research from the national research programme on crime at Vetenskapsrådet. Listen to the panel discussion on possible ways to counter recruitment, focusing on both traditional recruitment and recruitment online.

content.title: The climate transition as preparedness – what requirements are needed in planning, design and procurement?
content.description: How can climate action also strengthen resilience in Sweden’s municipalities? How can planning, design and procurement in the built environment be driven by resource efficiency, energy efficiency and circularity – while reducing vulnerability in everyday life and in a crisis?
content.extendedDescription: Resilience is not built after the fact – it is shaped by early choices. This seminar connects the climate transition with preparedness: material and energy efficiency, circular flows, resilient system solutions and investment decisions that remain sound even when circumstances change. We examine which requirements and incentives steer us in the wrong direction today (such as price-per-hour logic, micromanagement and short-term calculations) and what needs to change so that more projects deliver both a lower climate impact and greater resilience. The focus is on concrete policy and commissioning choices in planning, design and procurement.

content.title: A changing rental market – how does it affect segregation?
content.description: Large-scale renovations in the rental sector and privatisation of municipal public housing have changed Sweden’s rental market in recent decades. Differences in local conditions make the consequences for segregation a particularly relevant issue.
content.extendedDescription:
Large-scale renovations in the rental sector and privatisation of municipal public housing have changed Sweden’s rental market in recent decades. Renovations often lead to rent increases, while privatisation reduces or removes one of the tools municipalities have available to offer good housing to all income groups. Together, these processes can affect which households can remain in their rented homes and how the population is distributed across different neighbourhoods.

At the same time, renovations and privatisation are taking place at different rates and on different scales in Swedish municipalities. This creates varying local conditions and makes the consequences for segregation a particularly relevant issue.

This seminar discusses two research articles that shed light on these changes. Questions include: Who stays when rents rise after a renovation? Which households move? How does the social composition change in municipalities where public housing has been privatised?

content.title: The electric car transition – how can Sweden take the lead again?
content.description: Electrification of the transport sector is a central part of climate action and a strategic issue for Swedish industry. Electric cars are the only segment that is growing, despite an overall decline in passenger car sales. Even so, the transition to electric cars has not progressed as quickly as expected.
content.extendedDescription: Uncertainty about policy instruments, infrastructure and long-term rules risks delaying necessary investment. The seminar discusses why the transition to electric cars is necessary and natural, what lies behind the slowdown and what action is needed at political, industrial and societal levels for Sweden to regain its leadership in electrification.

content.title: Research in close partnership with industry – how Swedish games research can strengthen the games industry
content.description: The Swedish games industry has a unique opportunity to grow. Research, innovation and skills development can further strengthen its competitiveness. How should Swedish games research conducted in close partnership with industry develop to achieve these goals?
content.extendedDescription:
The Swedish games industry has a unique opportunity to grow regionally, nationally and globally. Through investment in research, innovation and skills development, the industry can strengthen its competitiveness, create sustainable business models and benefit from new technology.
In December 2025, KK-stiftelsen awarded SEK 29 million to develop a centre for Swedish games research (Game Development Research Center). This centre is an important step towards closer research collaboration between developers and researchers.

In this seminar, we invite those interested to discuss which research areas are most relevant and interesting. Small studios make up 90% of the industry, and an important question is how collaboration can be designed so that they too can benefit substantially from the research. A panel of games researchers and industry representatives discusses how this initiative should develop to reach different parts of the industry for constructive collaboration.

A light lunch will be provided!

content.title: Economic inequality is growing – how are children affected?
content.description: The gap between rich and poor is widening in Sweden, and the country’s very richest have almost doubled their share of income since the early 90s, according to Statistikmyndigheten SCB. How did the world’s most equal country get here? And what are the consequences for children?
content.extendedDescription:
A panel debate with politicians and experts on the societal challenges arising from growing economic inequality. Aid organisations report increasing demand, including from families with children, and researchers warn of increased crime and tensions as the gaps widen. What consequences does growing inequality have for society as a whole? How are children affected by greater differences in economic prosperity?
Historically, Sweden has sought to use redistributive policies to reduce differences in the conditions in which children grow up. Is this still the case? And if so, how well does society live up to that ambition?

content.title: In the global race for tech – how can Sweden secure jobs, innovation and competitiveness?
content.description: Sweden has long been a leader in technology and innovation, but this is not a position we can take for granted. With global changes, trade tariffs and tougher international competition, creating advanced technology such as AI, rather than only using it, is becoming crucial to job creation.
content.extendedDescription: This seminar will discuss the link between Swedish technology development and competitiveness. How is innovation translated into industrial growth? How can we future-proof the Swedish automotive industry and other technology sectors facing similar conditions? What role does collaboration between business, academia and policymakers play in ensuring that Sweden remains a leading technology nation?

content.title: A cultural heritage forum focusing on sensitive renovation and World Heritage
content.description: To address climate change, the EU has identified a need for innovation in the sustainable management and development of Europe’s existing building stock. How can local dialogue connect with an international research community?
content.extendedDescription:
To address climate change, the EU has identified a need for innovation in the sustainable management and development of Europe’s existing building stock. This event presents lessons from three ongoing EU-funded projects in which local dialogue in Visby connects with an international research community.
World Heritage sites are places that make a difference in their local communities and in the world.
There are more than 1200 World Heritage sites worldwide, and 15 of them are in Sweden. World Heritage belongs to everyone and forms part of the societies of the future through place development. The exhibitions introduce the World Heritage site Hansestaden Visby and the other 14 sites, and how they work with sustainable development and UNESCO’s vision of peace.
Burmeisterska huset is a meeting place for discussion and networking on cultural heritage and World Heritage issues. Exhibitions in the different rooms on the ground floor of this well-preserved house from the 1600s address several subjects relating to sensitive renovation of historic environments and sustainable place development at World Heritage sites.

content.title: How do we balance nuclear safety and electricity supply during heightened alert and war?
content.description: Developments in Ukraine show that, during heightened alert and warlike conditions, authorities and industry need to take measures that involve balancing radiation safety and electricity supply. How can this best be done without jeopardising either safety or access to electricity?

content.title: Participation as a protective factor – how does having a say affect young people’s mental health?
content.description: Many reports indicate that mental ill health among young people is increasing. A sense of coherence, belonging and the ability to influence one’s own life are crucial factors in wellbeing. The question is therefore not only how young people are feeling, but also what role participation plays in their wellbeing.
content.extendedDescription:
When young people feel that their voices are taken seriously – at school, in society and in decisions affecting their everyday lives – their sense of empowerment grows. Participation can act as a protective factor against mental ill health by contributing to a sense of meaning, responsibility and social belonging. But when young people feel that decisions are made over their heads, the opposite may happen: feelings of powerlessness, frustration and exclusion.

At the same time, participation is not always straightforward. It requires structures that make genuine influence possible, beyond symbolism. This means creating forums where young people can participate, but also ensuring that adults are prepared to listen, change and sometimes relinquish control.

In this roundtable discussion, we want to explore the link between participation and mental health.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: Who will work in public welfare services?
content.description: A staffing crisis in public welfare services. Female-dominated occupations in which pay, status and the working environment are lagging behind. It is becoming increasingly difficult to find people who want to work in health and social care. At the same time, many foreign-born people working in public welfare services face deportation. What needs to be done to meet staffing needs?
content.extendedDescription:
A panel debate with politicians and experts about the major challenges facing Sweden’s welfare sector. Demographic trends mean fewer people will have to support more as the proportion of older people increases.
Meanwhile, we are already seeing soaring staff turnover in social services and an elderly care sector with a poor reputation that struggles to attract staff. Migration policies also mean that many people working in public welfare services may be forced to leave the country.
A challenging working environment, high sickness absence, lagging pay and low status characterise health and social care occupations.
How does the fact that these are female-dominated occupations affect their status? How is their status affected by society’s view of older people?
Do politicians take these difficulties seriously? What does the welfare sector need to do to attract employees who will have the stamina to stay in their jobs in the future?
speakerTitles: Deputy Chief Executive of the Association

content.title: How do you live with mental ill health in a world of high achievement and polished appearances?
content.description: Feeling well and performing at your best cannot be taken for granted. More and more people live with mental health difficulties that limit their lives. Have we lost the resilience to understand and handle life’s ups and downs? What is a good enough level of wellbeing? Are there shortcuts to getting there?
content.extendedDescription:
In today’s society, there is a growing tendency to believe that we know best how to help ourselves. Reports suggest that our mental health has deteriorated, and for some people the situation becomes unsustainable and requires professional help.

Today’s meeting offers an opportunity to discuss and reflect further on this and on how mental ill health affects life.
One question is whether, when a society places more emphasis on the individual than on the context they come from and belong to, a sense of exclusion can arise that in itself creates vulnerability. The pressure to be successful and happy sits uneasily with everyday strains and the unpredictability of the world around us.
Have the lessons that sustained earlier generations been lost?

Is life really easier for some people, or are there approaches that make things easier when life is tough? How can professional support make a difference, and is it available when needed? Is there help and support for relatives?
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: System requirement: Sustainability - Can games made in Sweden lead the way?
content.description: Sweden has many of the world’s best game creators and a long history of sustainability leadership. How can these strengths be combined to take the lead in driving innovation while safeguarding the planet and promoting social sustainability?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden’s games industry combines world-leading creativity and innovation with deep-rooted values of environmental and social sustainability. From indie studios to global publishers, Swedish creators are already lowering their carbon footprint, ensuring safe and inclusive gameplay, building diverse workplaces, and designing games that inspire real-world change. But how can these efforts scale and what role must policy, research, and collaboration play?

This is not a drill. With seven of nine planetary boundaries crossed and just four years left to meet the 2030 Global Sustainability Goals, real action and bold leadership are urgently needed. There are no games on a dead planet. The path forward demands joint action across industries, creators, research, advocacy, and NGOs. Policymakers must create the conditions for success. This panel brings together all these perspectives to discuss how we can turn ambition into action for a safe and playful future.
speakerTitles: Lecturer and Researcher in Game Design

content.description: Today, the high investment cost of electric construction machinery and heavy trucks is an obstacle to the climate transition. How can innovative procurement overcome these obstacles?

content.title: How can Europe build digital sovereignty and resilience without losing competitiveness?
content.description: Digital sovereignty places new demands on companies and public institutions to control critical functions and ensure alternative solutions when IT systems face cyberattacks. But is it realistic for Europe to control the entire IT stack without losing competitiveness?
content.extendedDescription:
Danska ambassaden i Sverige invites you to a panel discussion with some of the strongest voices on digital sovereignty and resilience from research, public administration, government agencies and leading IT suppliers.

The discussion will address questions including:
• What does being digital fundamentally mean? Does it make us more vulnerable?
• Which areas can be outsourced, and which should remain in-house?
• What does the increased focus on resilience mean for collaboration with IT suppliers?
• How do we avoid vendor lock-in?
• How do we manage critical functions when the IT system goes down?

The discussion draws on knowledge and experience from both Denmark and Sweden and is moderated by Morten Friis Møller, digitalisation diplomat at the Danish embassy.

content.title: The empathy crisis – what happens when we stop caring?
content.description: Nordic societies have long been built on trust and care for one another. This has provided a foundation for stability, prosperity and strong cohesion. Today, however, public debate is increasingly dominated by narratives of crisis. What happens to a society when a sense of constant crisis takes over?
content.extendedDescription:
Research shows that when we feel anxious or believe we are living through a crisis, our capacity for empathy decreases. The consequences go beyond reduced humanitarian engagement or fewer resources for the world’s most vulnerable people. Such developments also risk affecting our own societies and the social fabric on which they rest.
Are we already seeing signs of this in reduced international engagement and a weaker willingness to help people globally? What happens to cohesion in our own societies when fear shapes policy more than facts? At the same time, we are confronted daily with images of war, violence and disasters. Do we risk becoming desensitised?
How can the media and public institutions report on crises without contributing to resignation and indifference? And how can we rebuild empathy in societies increasingly shaped by narratives of crisis?
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: National interest versus local veto – how do we break the deadlock in the energy transition?
content.description: Sweden’s green transition requires massive electricity production, but major infrastructure projects often founder on municipal vetoes and local opposition. How can we bridge the gap between national goals and local politics? What incentives exist, and what difference can early dialogue and better, data-driven decision support make?
content.extendedDescription:
Industry’s climate transition and Sweden’s future competitiveness depend entirely on a rapid, large-scale expansion of fossil-free electricity generation. Yet we see project after project halted at the last minute by municipal vetoes or shifting local opinion. The system creates enormous uncertainty and drives up costs for energy companies.

In this panel discussion, we focus on how to break the deadlock in permitting processes. What would make municipalities willing to say yes? We debate proposals for new financial incentives for local communities, the importance of building trust much earlier in the process, and how transparent political data can prevent conflicts. We also highlight how technology and systematic monitoring of external developments can help the energy sector navigate the local landscape more effectively.

A solution-focused discussion with representatives from the energy industry.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Make the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities law – for every young person with a disability’s right to a life
content.description: Today, young people with disabilities are excluded from large parts of social life, and many are prevented from participating in society on equal terms with other children and young people. In 2024, the UN criticised Sweden as the first country in the world to move backwards on disability rights. We need change now.
content.extendedDescription: The event would address the need to ensure that Sweden truly meets its commitments and that the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities becomes law. This would require Sweden to work actively to counter discrimination, improve accessibility and ensure that society is inclusive at every level – in schools, the labour market, healthcare and housing. It would create a legal foundation making it harder to implement decisions that restrict rights. Sweden has been criticised at the UN for failing to live up to the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities despite ratifying it. Sweden is the first country ever to be criticised for moving backwards on the rights of people with disabilities, and this affects children and young people with disabilities first and most severely. A seminar consisting of a panel discussion with youth organisations, disability organisations and legal experts, discussing and highlighting different perspectives on why

content.title: The world’s best at sustainability – what can Sweden learn from Lund?
content.description: The climate transition requires more than ambition. How do we create real change in large organisations? What is required of leadership, research and collaboration to turn words into action, and what can businesses and public authorities learn from academia?
content.extendedDescription:
Lunds universitet tops the QS World University Rankings: Sustainability 2026 as the world’s leading university in sustainability. But what lies behind that position – and what can others learn from it?

This panel discussion brings together academia, public authorities and business to discuss what it takes to succeed with long-term, systematic sustainability work. What does it mean to work strategically on sustainability in large organisations? What priorities and forms of leadership are needed?

The discussion draws on experience from Lund – where the university, public bodies and companies have worked on sustainability in research, policy development and innovation for a long time – while also placing it in a national context. Which lessons are relevant to other Swedish organisations seeking a leading role in the transition? And how can research help accelerate progress towards a more sustainable society?

content.title: Cooperation between Swedish municipalities, regions, organisations and their counterparts in Ukraine
content.description: Sweden’s support for Ukraine is often based on cooperation between the public sector and civil society organisations. These partnerships can strengthen humanitarian support, reconstruction and knowledge exchange to the benefit of all parties. How does this work in practice, and what impact does it have?
content.extendedDescription:
We explore how public bodies and volunteer organisations can join forces to support both communities and organisations in Ukraine. We highlight several examples, including partnerships supporting Gammalsvenskby, Fastiv and Poltava.

How do regions, municipalities, volunteer organisations and recipients in Ukraine work together? How can volunteer organisations enable regions and municipalities to send donations to Ukraine?

Is the cooperation one-sided, or does Sweden benefit from the exchange? Why should municipalities and regions invest in this type of cooperation?

content.title: How do the soldiers on the Ukrainian front line see the war through their eyes?
content.description: How do soldiers on the front line—after long periods in trenches, fighting for freedom—see and experience the war? What do they feel and witness?
content.extendedDescription:
The exhibition Through Their Eyes brings together two powerful projects — Chasiv Yar. – Fireproof and the award-winning Frontline Rolls — revealing the reality of war through the eyes of Ukrainian soldiers.

Chasiv Yar. – Fireproof is dedicated to the defense of Chasiv Yar by soldiers of the 24th Separate Mechanized Brigade named after King Danylo. The photographs are displayed on fragments of a fence from the Donetsk region, damaged by Russian shelling, as well as within the exhibition tent — grounding the images directly in the material reality of war.

Frontline Rolls — winner of the 2026 PHMuseum Prize — offers a deeply personal insight into the lives and inner worlds of soldiers on the front line. By sending disposable film cameras to different sections of the front line, project author Sergey Melnitchenko gave soldiers the opportunity to document their own reality. The result is a unique archive of wartime testimonies.

Visiting Ukrainian officers from the front line guide you!

content.title: Preparedness and security – what leadership strengthens society’s resilience?
content.description: At a time of growing security tensions and rapid changes in the world around us, preparedness and resilience are becoming increasingly important for society, organisations and businesses. What leadership is needed to create a secure future – among established leaders and the younger generation?
content.extendedDescription:
In this seminar, participants meet in an Open Space format, where questions, perspectives and experiences from the audience help shape the conversation. The focus is on exploring together how organisations can strengthen their preparedness and ability to act in complex, changing situations.

Experienced leaders facilitate the discussions, focusing on leadership in times of uncertainty and on cooperation, mandates and the allocation of responsibilities. We bring different perspectives together to develop a broader understanding of how preparedness can be improved.

Examples of questions explored:
• How should a leader act and take responsibility to create a safer future?
• What does preparedness mean in practice for organisations today?
• What does it take for leaders to stand by their values while building collective strength within their organisations?
• What does a sustainable leadership role look like when awareness of crises is constantly heightened?
• What do organisations need to do to strengthen their resilience?

content.title: Ukraine–Sweden cooperation: strengthening civil protection and emergency response
content.description: What role do rescue services play in civil defence during wartime? How can a cooperation between Rescue Services South East and Poltava strengthen preparedness and mutual learning?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden needs to strengthen its civil defence capabilities. How can international cooperation strengthen resilience in times of crisis? Rescue Services South East works closely with emergency services in Poltava, Ukraine – Kalmar’s twin city. Through exchanges, study visits and donations of equipment, the partnership creates valuable knowledge transfer.
For Sweden, this provides unique insight into emergency response under extreme conditions such as war and infrastructure disruption. For Poltava, the situation is highly demanding, with increased pressure, damaged facilities and limited resources while ensuring safety for both personnel and civilians. You will meet the responsible persons for this cooperation and the Swedish Minister for Civil Defence will present his perspective on how cooperation with Ukraine can strengthen preparedness. 
The panel will also include a minute of silence to honour injured and fallen personnel in rescue and health services.

content.title: The Sound of War: How Drone Noise Shapes Youth Trauma in Ukraine
content.description: War-related sounds such as drones, sirens and explosions can cause long-term trauma in children and youth. This issue highlights how sensory experiences of war affect mental health, integration and recovery long after conflict and displacement have ended.
content.extendedDescription:
This panel discussion explores the long-term psychological impact of war-related sounds on children and young people affected by the war in Ukraine. While the physical consequences of war are widely recognized, the effects of constant exposure to drone noise, air raid sirens, explosions, and other sounds associated with danger receive less attention. Research and lived experiences show that such sounds can become powerful trauma triggers, affecting mental health, learning, sleep, and social well-being long after the immediate threat has passed.

The discussion will examine how sound functions as a form of psychological stress in modern warfare, how auditory trauma can persist after displacement, and what lessons can be drawn from both contemporary and historical conflicts. The format is a moderated panel discussion followed by audience questions. No prior preparation is required from participants.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: From separate parts to a whole – future care and support for people with harmful substance use and dependence
content.description: The government has decided to begin implementing the co-occurring conditions reform – a reform aimed at more integrated care for everyone with harmful substance use or dependence and those with co-occurring conditions. The first legislative amendments are due to take effect on 1 January 2028.
content.extendedDescription:
In January 2025, the government appointed Samsjuklighetsdelegationen to assist Regeringskansliet in implementing the co-occurring conditions reform, with a clear mandate to take the first step as soon as possible. The reform is based on proposals from Samsjuklighetsutredningen (SOU 2021:93, SOU 2023:5) and will bring far-reaching changes to care for people with harmful substance use or dependence. In April 2026, the government decided on a bill proposing a new law and several legislative amendments for more consistent and integrated care for people with harmful substance use or dependence, with more specific proposals for people with co-occurring psychiatric conditions.

The seminar presents Samsjuklighetsdelegationen’s remit and work on the reform. Together with experts, it highlights different perspectives: children and young people, adults, service users and relatives. This is followed by a panel discussion with politicians and others focusing on implementation of the reform.

content.title: Girls in crisis – who takes responsibility?
content.description: Mental ill health among girls and young women is rising rapidly. At the same time, healthcare overlooks many girls with ADHD, who are diagnosed several years later than boys. This increases the risk of anxiety, dependence and vulnerability. How can healthcare become more equitable – and what political action is needed to reverse the trend?
content.extendedDescription:
Mental ill health among girls and young women is rising rapidly, while neurodevelopmental diagnoses such as ADHD and autism are becoming more common. Research shows that girls with ADHD are diagnosed several years later than boys on average. During this time, many develop secondary problems such as anxiety, self-harm, eating disorders, alcohol and drug problems, and destructive relationships.
Studies also show clear links between ADHD, alcohol use and sexual risk-taking among girls and young women. Women with ADHD are also at greater risk than men of developing dependence before diagnosis, but are less likely to receive treatment.
Although hormonal cycles affect the brain’s response to alcohol, drugs and medication, healthcare still often treats boys and men as the norm. This can lead to delayed diagnosis and inappropriate or absent treatment.
The seminar discusses the links between undetected ADHD, mental ill health and dependence – and what political decisions are needed to reverse the trend.
speakerTitles: Associate Professor, Senior Consultant in Psychiatry

content.title: Everyone is talking about PPP – but how are Private-Public Partnerships created in practice?
content.description: More and more people are discussing cooperation between public authorities and private businesses within Sweden’s total defence. An increasingly common term is dual-use, where the same resources are shared between defence and civilian society. But how are PPPs created and maintained in practice? Who leads? Who does the work?
content.extendedDescription: What does an optimal PPP look like? What does research say about PPPs? How is cooperation organised in other countries? Do we have a regulatory framework that encourages cooperation? Who has responsibility, and who takes responsibility within PPPs? A panel of experienced representatives from different parts of society attempts to answer these questions.

content.title: Can we avoid the mistakes of 1973?
content.description: The oil crisis of 1973 triggered a prolonged economic downturn and radically changed architecture. Energy savings took precedence over light, space and flexibility – think thick walls and windows like arrow slits. Today, we see the consequences in extensive alterations that are very difficult and expensive to carry out.
content.extendedDescription: How do we avoid mistakes this time and create buildings that stand the test of time? Because the most sustainable things we can build are places people want to keep.
